analysis.one_liner: Bans a hormone-disrupting plastic chemical (BPA) from products for young children.
analysis.headline: The BPA-Free Kids Act was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee and never received a hearing or vote before the 110th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would treat any children's product — for kids seven or younger — that contains a detectable amount of bisphenol A (BPA), a chemical used in some hard plastics and can linings, as a banned hazardous substance under federal consumer-safety law. It would also order the CDC to study BPA's health effects across all age groups and in pregnant women, and it would leave states free to pass their own stricter rules.
analysis.who_benefits: Parents and young children, who would no longer be exposed to BPA through baby bottles, sippy cups, toys, and other products made for young kids; pregnant women, who would get new federal research on how BPA exposure affects them and their pregnancies; and state governments, which could keep or adopt stricter BPA rules of their own.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Parents of young children and pregnant women

how_it_helps.text: Beginning 180 days after enactment, any product made for or marketed to a child age seven or younger that contains a detectable amount of BPA would be treated as a banned hazardous substance, taking it off the market under the Federal Hazardous Substances Act.

The bill directs the CDC to submit a plan within 90 days for a study of BPA's health effects in all age groups and in pregnant women, building the scientific record on a chemical Americans are widely exposed to.
States and localities may keep or adopt BPA rules that provide equal or greater protection, so the federal ban sets a floor rather than blocking tougher state laws.

analysis.who_pays: Manufacturers of children's products and the chemical companies that produce BPA, who would have to reformulate products for young children to eliminate BPA or lose those product lines. Companies would bear compliance costs, which could be passed partly to consumers through prices.

drawbacks.text: The standard is strict: it bans any detectable amount of BPA with no safe threshold written in, so manufacturers would have to remove it entirely rather than stay under a limit.

Companies making baby bottles, sippy cups, and other children's products would face reformulation and testing costs on relatively short notice (the ban takes effect 180 days after enactment), a cost an honest supporter would acknowledge even while arguing it is justified for children's health.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit — removing a hormone-disrupting chemical from products used by infants and young children — is targeted and directly protective, while the cost is limited to reformulating a defined set of children's products; the bill even allows stricter state laws, so it sets a floor rather than a ceiling. The main design criticism is that a zero-detectable-amount standard with no threshold gives manufacturers no margin, but for products made for very young children, that strictness is the point.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in April 2008 and referred to the Senate Commerce Committee, which never took it up — no hearing, no vote, no further action — before the Congress ended in January 2009.

narrative.text: Senator Chuck Schumer introduced the BPA-Free Kids Act of 2008 on April 29, 2008, joined by Senator Feinstein, Senator Clinton, Senator Durbin, Senator Kerry, and Senator Menendez as original cosponsors.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation the same day; that referral was the last action of any kind in the record.
Eleven senators cosponsored the bill — 10 Democrats and 1 Independent — but it never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote before the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Manufacturers that continued selling BPA-containing children's products and the chemical producers that supply BPA were better off, since no federal ban ever took effect. Parents and young children got no federal protection from this bill, and the question was left to states acting on their own.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: BPA producers and children's product makers

for.name: Sen. Chuck Schumer
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on April 29, 2008, to ban BPA from products made for children seven and younger.

for.name: Sen. Dianne Feinstein, Hillary Clinton, Richard Durbin, John Kerry, and Robert Menendez
for.what_they_did: Joined as original cosponsors when the bill was introduced, bringing total cosponsor support to 11 senators (10 Democrats, 1 Independent).

against.name: Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral on April 29, 2008, and took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no committee vote — for the rest of the 110th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 12 senators behind the bill — the sponsor plus 11 cosponsors — were Democrats or an Independent; no Republican cosponsor appears in the record, and the bill never reached a vote where partisan splits could be measured.

industries.note: These companies supply bisphenol A to makers of hard plastics and food packaging; a federal ban in children's products would have cut off a set of customers and opened the door to broader restrictions. The public's interest in removing a hormone-disrupting chemical from children's products runs against this industry's interest in keeping BPA sales.

industries.industry: Baby bottle, sippy cup, and children's product manufacturers
industries.note: Makers of polycarbonate bottles and other children's items would have had to reformulate or drop BPA-containing lines within 180 days of enactment. Some children's brands had already begun marketing BPA-free products, so a federal ban would partly have leveled costs among competitors.

Retailers would face stocking and compliance questions about which products contain detectable BPA, but many had already pulled BPA bottles in response to consumer demand; a clear federal rule replaces a patchwork of state standards the bill expressly preserves.
